title: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
summary: How stack frames and malloc really get memory, how x86-64 walks a 4-level page table bit by bit, why TLB reach and huge pages matter, and how page faults make allocation lazy.
outcomes: Trace how call, ret and rsp create and free stack frames, and estimate how deep recursion can go
Compute the chunk size glibc malloc uses for a request and explain brk versus mmap allocation
Split an x86-64 virtual address into page-table indices and offset for 4 KiB and 2 MiB pages
Compute TLB reach and explain when huge pages, PCIDs and TLB shootdowns matter
Explain minor and major page faults, copy-on-write fork and Linux overcommit

lessons.title: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns

blocks.md: Every running function needs scratch space: its arguments, its local variables, and the address to jump back to when it finishes. Function calls nest and unwind in strict last-in, first-out (LIFO) order: if `main` calls `sum`, `sum` must finish before `main` resumes. A **stack** is the data structure that matches that order exactly, so every process gets one, managed directly by the CPU's call instructions.

On x86-64, register `rsp` (the **stack pointer**) holds the address of the top of the stack, and the stack grows toward **lower** addresses. The `call` instruction pushes the return address (subtract 8 from `rsp`, store), and `ret` pops it back. A function then reserves room for its locals with a single subtraction from `rsp`. That block of memory, from the return address down to the new `rsp`, is the function's **stack frame**. Unoptimized code also saves the caller's `rbp` (the **frame pointer**, a register pointing at the current frame) in a short entry sequence called the **prologue**.

blocks.caption: A tiny recursive function. Unoptimized builds give each call its own frame; with optimization a compiler may turn this recursion into a loop and use no extra frames.

blocks.title: Frames pile up, then unwind

scenes.caption: Simplified model: each sum frame is 32 bytes (return address, saved rbp, the local rest, padding). Before main's call, rsp = 0x7ffe1000, a multiple of 16 as the ABI requires.
call sum(2) pushes the return address, the prologue saves rbp and subtracts 16. The whole frame costs a few instructions, no matter how many locals it holds.
sum(1) gets a fresh frame 32 bytes lower. Each call has its own n and rest, which is why recursion works at all.
sum(0) is the deepest frame. rsp is now 0x60 = 96 bytes below where main started.
sum(0) returns 0. ret pops the return address and rsp moves back up: freeing the frame was just pointer arithmetic, nothing was erased.
sum(1) returns 1 to sum(2), which computes 2 + 1.
Back in main, rsp is 0x7ffe1000 again. All three frames are gone in O(1) each, with no bookkeeping.

blocks.title: The same stack, 8 bytes per cell

scenes.caption: Addresses 0x7ffe0ff8 down to 0x7ffe0fa0, only the low 12 bits shown. Nothing is in use yet; rsp sits at 0x7ffe1000, just above the left edge.
sum(2): return address into main, saved rbp, its local rest and 8 bytes of padding that keep rsp 16-byte aligned.
sum(1) and sum(0) stack their frames below. The stack only ever grows and shrinks at one end.
After two returns rsp is back at 0x7ffe0fe0. The old bytes of the dead frames are still there (muted): the next call simply overwrites them.

blocks.md: Two ABI rules from the System V x86-64 psABI shape every frame. First, `rsp` must be 16-byte aligned just before a `call`, so frames are padded to multiples of 16. Second, the 128 bytes just below `rsp`, the **red zone**, are reserved: signal and interrupt handlers must not touch them, so a leaf function (one that calls nothing) may keep its whole frame there without moving `rsp` at all.

blocks.prompt: The default stack size limit on many Linux systems is 8 MiB (`ulimit -s` prints 8192). With 32-byte frames as in our model, roughly how deep can `sum` recurse before the program crashes?
blocks.reveal: About $8 \times 2^{20} / 32 = 262,144$ frames (minus whatever main and the C runtime already use). Then the next push touches memory below the limit and the process gets **SIGSEGV**, a *stack overflow*. Real frames are often larger than 32 bytes, so the real limit is lower. This is why deep recursion over untrusted input (say, parsing deeply nested JSON) is a classic crash bug.

blocks.md: Where the limits come from on Linux: the main thread's stack grows on demand, up to the `RLIMIT_STACK` resource limit ([getrlimit(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrlimit.2.html)); hitting it raises SIGSEGV. The kernel also keeps a guard gap below the stack where no other mapping may be placed, 256 pages by default (1 MiB with 4 KiB pages). Other threads get a **fixed-size** stack chosen at creation: with glibc it defaults to the `RLIMIT_STACK` soft limit, or 2 MB on most architectures if that limit is unlimited ([pthread_create(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_create.3.html)).

The stack is not faster *memory*. Stack and heap bytes live in the same RAM behind the same caches. What is cheaper is *allocation*: one `sub` on `rsp` versus a search through allocator data structures. The top of the stack is also almost always hot in cache because it is reused constantly.

Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

blocks.question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
blocks.explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

blocks.question: Why can a leaf function on x86-64 Linux often skip adjusting `rsp` entirely?
options: Leaf functions run in kernel mode and use the kernel stack
The CPU automatically allocates a frame on every call
Leaf functions cannot have local variables
The 128-byte red zone below rsp is guaranteed not to be clobbered by signal or interrupt handlers
blocks.explain: The psABI reserves 128 bytes below `rsp` that handlers must not modify. A function that calls nothing can keep its locals there, since no callee will push into that space. Saving the `sub`/`add` pair is a small win on very hot leaf functions.

lessons.title: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory

blocks.md: Some data cannot live on the stack: its size is only known at run time, it must outlive the function that created it, or it is too large for a bounded stack. That data goes on the **heap**, a region managed by a user-space library (`malloc` and `free` in C). The library hands out pieces of a big region and takes them back in *any* order, which is exactly what makes it harder than a stack.

Because blocks are freed in arbitrary order, free space ends up scattered. An allocator tracks it in a **free list** and relies on two mechanisms (OSTEP ch. 17). **Splitting**: to serve a small request from a bigger free chunk, cut the chunk in two and keep the remainder on the list. **Coalescing**: when a chunk is freed, merge it with free neighbours so large requests can still succeed.

scenes.caption: OSTEP's example heap of 30 bytes, drawn as six 5-byte cells. Bytes 0 to 9 and 20 to 29 are free, 10 to 19 are in use. The free list holds two 10-byte entries.
A request for 15 bytes fails even though 20 bytes are free in total: no single free chunk is big enough. That is external fragmentation.
malloc(1) is served by splitting the chunk at 20: byte 20 is returned, and the free entry becomes address 21, length 9 (cell 20-24 now mixed).
Back to the original heap, now free(10). Without coalescing the list shows three 10-byte chunks and a 20-byte request still fails.
With coalescing the freed chunk merges with both neighbours into a single 30-byte chunk, so any request up to 30 bytes can succeed.

blocks.md: Real allocators also need to know a block's size when you call `free(p)`, which gets no size argument. glibc's malloc stores it in a hidden header word just before the pointer it returns. From the comments in glibc's `malloc.c`: on 64-bit systems the alignment is 16 bytes, each in-use chunk carries 8 bytes of overhead, and the minimum chunk is 32 bytes, so even `malloc(0)` consumes 32 bytes. The rounding rule is the `request2size` macro:

blocks.caption: glibc request2size on 64-bit: add the 8-byte header, round up to a multiple of 16, never below the 32-byte minimum. Usable size is chunk minus 8.

blocks.title: What a small malloc really costs (glibc, 64-bit)

scenes.caption: Bytes requested by the program.

Chunk size glibc carves from the heap, computed with request2size. 24 bytes fit in the 32-byte minimum because the next chunk's prev_size field, unused while your chunk is in use, is lent to you; 25 bytes tips into 48.
Bytes consumed beyond the request: 31 bytes for a 1-byte malloc. Millions of tiny heap objects pay this tax, which is why pools and arenas exist.

blocks.md:
Where does the heap get memory from the kernel? glibc uses two routes ([malloc(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/malloc.3.html), [mallopt(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/mallopt.3.html)):

- **Small requests** come from the main heap, grown by moving the *program break* with `brk`/`sbrk`. Freed chunks go on free lists for reuse, and the heap can only be trimmed from its top end.
- **Large requests** (at least `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD`, 128 KiB by default) that the free lists cannot satisfy get their own private anonymous `mmap`. `free` returns them to the kernel immediately, but each one costs system calls and kernel page zeroing.

The threshold is dynamic by default: when a mmap-backed block larger than the current threshold (and at most 32 MiB on 64-bit) is freed, glibc raises the threshold to that size, betting that the program will keep allocating blocks that big. Multithreaded programs add one more layer: to avoid lock contention glibc creates extra **arenas**, separate heaps with their own mutexes, and keeps a small per-thread cache of recently freed chunks.

`free` rarely shrinks your process. Freed small chunks go back on glibc's free lists, not to the kernel, and a single live chunk near the top of the heap blocks trimming. A process whose memory never drops after a burst is usually not leaking; check whether the memory is reusable before hunting leaks.
Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

blocks.question: On 64-bit glibc, how many heap bytes does `malloc(25)` consume?
blocks.explain: request2size computes (25 + 8 + 15) rounded down to a multiple of 16 = 48. The 8-byte header pushes 25 bytes past the 32-byte minimum chunk, whose usable size is only 24.

blocks.question: A server allocates and frees many 200 KiB buffers. After the first one is freed, later allocations of the same size stop showing up as mmap calls in strace. Why?
options: The dynamic mmap threshold rose to the size of the freed block, so new 200 KiB requests are served from the heap
glibc caches the mmap call result in the kernel
200 KiB is below the default 128 KiB threshold
The kernel merged the mappings into the stack
blocks.explain: Freeing an mmap-backed block larger than the current threshold (but at most the 32 MiB cap on 64-bit) raises the threshold to that size. From then on 200 KiB requests come from the brk heap and its free lists, avoiding mmap, munmap and page zeroing on each cycle.

lessons.title: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit

blocks.md: Stack and heap addresses are **virtual**: the prerequisite course showed that a per-process page table maps virtual page numbers to physical frames, and that a multi-level tree keeps that table small. This lesson makes it exact for x86-64 with 4 KiB pages, so you can take any 64-bit pointer and say precisely which table entries the hardware reads.

The numbers come from the page size. A 4 KiB page needs a 12-bit **offset** ($2^{12} = 4096$). Each page-table node is itself one 4 KiB page of 8-byte entries, so it holds 512 entries and is indexed by 9 bits. Four levels of 9 bits plus the 12-bit offset give $4 \times 9 + 12 = 48$ bits of virtual address. Linux names the levels PGD, PUD, PMD and PTE (a fifth level, P4D, is folded away when the hardware uses only four).

blocks.caption: How x86-64 4-level paging slices a virtual address. Index at each level = (address >> shift) mod 512 with shifts 39, 30, 21, 12.

blocks.md: Bits 63 to 48 are not translated; they must all equal bit 47. Addresses that obey this are **canonical**; anything else faults. That splits the 256 TiB space into two halves, and Linux's x86-64 memory map gives user space the lower one, `0` to `0x00007fffffffffff`, about 128 TiB per process. The kernel lives in the upper half.

scenes.caption: A typical user-space heap pointer, 0x00007f3a12345678. Bit 47 is 0 and bits 63 to 48 are all 0, so it is canonical.
(va >> 39) mod 512 = 254: entry 254 of the process's top-level table.
(va >> 30) mod 512 = 232 and (va >> 21) mod 512 = 145 pick entries in the next two tables.
(va >> 12) mod 512 = 325 selects the PTE. The low 12 bits, 0x678 = 1656, pass through untranslated.

blocks.title: The hardware page walk for one TLB miss

scenes.caption: CR3 holds the physical address of this process's top-level table. Switching processes means loading a different CR3.
Each step reads one 8-byte entry from memory to find the next table. Entry 254, then 232, then 145.
PTE entry 325 holds frame number 0x1a2b3 (a made-up value). Physical address = 0x1a2b3 x 4096 + 0x678 = 0x1a2b3678. Four dependent memory reads before the real access.
Huge page: if the PMD entry has its page-size bit set it maps a 2 MiB frame directly. The walk stops one level early and the low 21 bits, 0x145678, become the offset.

blocks.md: The same trick works one level higher: a PUD entry can map a 1 GiB page, leaving a 30-bit offset. Linux's documentation describes exactly this: on x86, 2M and 1G pages are mapped by entries in the second and third level tables. Each table level also tells you how much memory one full table covers: a PTE table maps $512 \times 4$ KiB = 2 MiB, a PMD table 1 GiB, a PUD table 512 GiB.

Newer CPUs add a fifth level ([5-level paging](https://docs.kernel.org/arch/x86/x86_64/5level-paging.html)): 9 more bits give 57-bit virtual addresses, 128 PiB in total and 56 bits for user space. A miss walks one more table. Linux still does not hand out user addresses above 47 bits by default, because some JIT compilers stash data in the high bits of pointers; a program opts in by passing a high hint address to `mmap`.

A miss does not always cost four DRAM reads. The page-table entries are ordinary data that can sit in the CPU caches, and Linux's page-table docs note that MMUs also keep page walk caches for upper levels. The four loads are the worst case of the structure, not a fixed latency.
Read a pointer as five numbers: four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset. Huge pages simply end the walk early and widen the offset to 21 or 30 bits.

blocks.question: For virtual address 0x00007f3a12345678 mapped with a 2 MiB huge page, which bits form the offset within the page?
options: Bits 11 to 0
Bits 20 to 0
Bits 29 to 0
Bits 47 to 21
blocks.explain: A 2 MiB page is $2^{21}$ bytes, so the offset is the low 21 bits (here 0x145678). The PMD entry maps the page directly, so bits 20 to 12, which would normally index a PTE table, become part of the offset.

blocks.question: A program maps 1 GiB of memory and touches all of it with 4 KiB pages. Roughly how much memory do the last-level page tables alone take?
options: 4 KiB
64 KiB
2 MiB
1 GiB
blocks.explain: 1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144 PTEs at 8 bytes each = 2 MiB, which is 512 PTE tables of 4 KiB. With 2 MiB pages the same gigabyte needs just 512 PMD entries, one 4 KiB table.

lessons.title: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns

blocks.md: A walk of four dependent loads on every access would be ruinous, so the MMU caches finished translations in the **translation lookaside buffer** (TLB). The prerequisite course covered hits and misses. Here the question is quantitative: how much memory can the TLB cover, what happens when your working set is bigger, and what flushes it.

**TLB reach** (OSTEP calls it coverage) is the memory a TLB can map at once: number of entries times page size. OSTEP's Culler's Law sums up the consequence: RAM isn't always RAM. If a program touches more pages in a short time than the TLB can hold, it takes miss after miss even when the data itself fits in cache.

blocks.caption: Model TLB of 1,024 entries. Real CPUs have several TLB levels with separate, model-specific sizes per page size.

blocks.title: Translation overhead vs working set (simple model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: uniformly random accesses, a fully associative TLB, hit rate = min(1, reach / working set), and a fixed walk cost (30 cycles here is an assumed value, not a measurement).
With 4 KiB pages the overhead appears past 4 MiB: at 64 MiB about 94 percent of accesses miss, costing about 28 extra cycles each in this model.
2 MiB pages push the knee out 512 times further, to 2 GiB. The same 64 MiB working set now never misses.
Quadrupling the TLB to 4,096 entries moves the 4 KiB knee only to 16 MiB. Huge pages scale reach far more cheaply than bigger TLBs.

blocks.md: Linux offers huge pages two ways ([concepts](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/concepts.html)). **hugetlbfs** needs an administrator to reserve huge pages up front and the application to map them explicitly; databases often do this. **Transparent Huge Pages** (THP) needs no code changes: the kernel uses 2 MiB pages for suitable anonymous memory when it can, and the `khugepaged` daemon collapses runs of small pages later. THP can be set to `always`, `madvise` (only regions marked with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)`) or `never`.

Huge pages are not free. The THP documentation warns that a process that maps a large region but touches one byte can get a whole 2 MiB page instead of 4 KiB, and allocating a huge page needs 2 MiB of *physically contiguous* memory, which may require compaction. That is why `madvise` mode exists.

The TLB also has to stay correct when mappings change. On a context switch the new process uses different page tables. The simple fix is to flush the whole TLB; OSTEP describes the better one, an **address space identifier** (ASID) tag on each entry. x86 calls it PCID: with it, Linux can switch page tables without flushing everything ([PTI docs](https://docs.kernel.org/arch/x86/pti.html)); without it, every CR3 write flushes the TLB.

Multithreaded programs add a harder case. Threads share one page table, so each CPU running a thread of the process may hold a cached translation. When one thread unmaps memory, the kernel must invalidate that translation everywhere before the memory can be reused. This is a **TLB shootdown**: in Linux's x86 code (`arch/x86/mm/tlb.c`) the initiating CPU sends inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) to the other CPUs using that address space and waits for them to finish flushing. Some newer AMD CPUs can instead broadcast the invalidation in hardware (INVLPGB), which current Linux uses when available.

scenes.caption: A thread unmaps a buffer. CPU 1 is running another thread of the same process and may have the old translation in its TLB.
The kernel clears the PTEs, then flushes its own TLB entries (one invlpg per page or a full flush, a tradeoff the kernel's x86 TLB docs discuss).
CPU 1 cannot see CPU 0's flush, so CPU 0 interrupts it with an IPI and waits. CPU 1 stops what it was doing to flush.
Only after the acknowledgement may the pages be reused and munmap return. The cost grows with the number of CPUs the process runs on.

blocks.md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

blocks.question: A random-access hash table grows from 2 MiB to 512 MiB and slows down more than its cache miss rate explains. Which change most directly targets the extra cost?
options: Use a TLB with twice as many entries
Switch from malloc to calloc
Increase RLIMIT_STACK
Back the table with 2 MiB huge pages (for example madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE))
blocks.explain: 512 MiB of random access is far beyond a 4 KiB-page TLB's reach, so most accesses also need a page walk. 2 MiB pages raise reach 512 times, so the table needs only 256 translations. You cannot buy a bigger TLB in software, and the other options do not touch translation.

blocks.question: Why is calling munmap on a small buffer often slower in a 64-thread process than in a single-threaded one?
options: The kernel must shoot down stale TLB entries on every CPU running the process, using IPIs and waiting for them
munmap must zero the pages first
Each thread has its own page table that must be edited
munmap takes a global lock across all processes
blocks.explain: Threads share one page table, so any CPU running one of them might cache the translation. The initiating CPU interrupts those CPUs and waits for them to flush before the pages can be reused. Threads do not have separate page tables, and freed pages are not zeroed at munmap.

lessons.title: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit

blocks.md: A **page fault** is the exception the MMU raises when a translation fails: the page is not present, or the access breaks its permissions. The prerequisite course treated it as the path to swapping. On modern Linux most faults are something else: the kernel's way of being **lazy**. Linux's page-table docs name the two common, expected causes: lazy allocation and copy-on-write.

When `malloc(64 MiB)` calls `mmap`, the kernel only records a new region of the address space (a virtual memory area); it does not allocate a single physical frame or fill a single PTE. The first touch of each page faults. The handler checks that the address lies inside a valid region with the right permissions, allocates a zeroed frame, installs the PTE and returns, and the CPU **retries** the faulting instruction, which now succeeds.

blocks.title: First touch of freshly malloc'ed memory

scenes.caption: malloc of 64 MiB becomes mmap. The kernel records the region and returns an address. No RAM is used yet.
The first store to p[0]: TLB miss, the page walk finds no present PTE, so the MMU raises a page fault.
The address is inside a valid writable region, so this is a minor fault: allocate a zeroed frame, fill the PTE, no disk I/O.
Return from the exception and retry the store, which now hits. The next 4 KiB page will fault again on its first touch.
A store to an address in no valid region (say a dangling pointer into unmapped memory) also faults, but the handler finds nothing to fix and sends SIGSEGV.

blocks.md: `getrusage(2)` counts both kinds of fault per process: `ru_minflt`, faults serviced without I/O, and `ru_majflt`, faults that needed I/O, such as reading a page back from swap or from a memory-mapped file. A minor fault costs a trip into the kernel and zeroing a page; a major fault waits for storage, which is far slower.

blocks.caption: Counting minor faults around a large malloc. Compile with `cc faults.c` on Linux.

blocks.prompt: Run the program above on Linux with 4 KiB pages and THP disabled. Roughly how many faults does the malloc line cause, and how many does the touch loop cause?
blocks.reveal: The malloc line causes about **1**: mmap only reserves address space, but glibc then writes its chunk header into the first page. The loop causes about $64\,\text{MiB} / 4\,\text{KiB} = 16,384$ minor faults, one per page on first write (one fewer because malloc already touched the first page, plus a few from the C library itself). With THP set to `always` and a suitably aligned region the kernel can fill 2 MiB per fault, as few as 32 faults, which is the 512x reduction the THP docs describe.

blocks.md: The same laziness makes `fork` cheap. The fork(2) man page says Linux implements it with **copy-on-write** pages: the child gets a copy of the parent's page tables, both pointing at the same frames, marked read-only. Only when either process writes to a page does a fault occur; the kernel then copies that one page and gives the writer a private, writable copy.

scenes.caption: Before fork: the parent's four virtual pages map frames F7, F2, F9 and F4 (made-up frame numbers).
After fork: the child's page table points at the very same frames and both sides are marked read-only. No data was copied.
The child writes to page 1: write to a read-only page, fault. The kernel copies F2 into a new frame F11 and maps it writable for the child only. The parent's F2 stays read-only for now.
If the child now calls exec, its old mappings, F11 included, are dropped. Only one 4 KiB page was ever copied, and the parent's next write to each page just makes it writable again, without copying.

blocks.md: Laziness has a consequence: the kernel hands out more address space than it has RAM, known as **overcommit**. Linux's overcommit accounting has three modes set by `vm.overcommit_memory`: 0 (the default) refuses only obvious overcommits (in the kernel's [mm/util.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/mm/util.c), a single request larger than total RAM plus swap); 1 always overcommits; 2 never does, capping total commitments at swap plus a ratio of RAM (50 percent by default). In modes 0 and 1, if pages actually get touched and memory runs out, the **OOM killer** terminates processes to recover.

A non-NULL return from `malloc` does not mean the memory exists. Under default overcommit a large allocation succeeds immediately, and the failure, if any, comes later as an OOM kill when the pages are first written, far from the line that allocated them.

Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

blocks.question: A 10 GiB Redis-like process calls fork to write a snapshot while it keeps serving writes. Memory use climbs sharply during the snapshot. Why?
options: fork copies all 10 GiB up front
The child process leaks heap memory
Every page the parent writes while the child holds the old version triggers a copy-on-write fault and a new private copy
Copy-on-write is disabled for anonymous memory
blocks.explain: fork only duplicates page tables. But each page the parent modifies during the snapshot must be copied so the child still sees the old data, so memory grows with the number of distinct pages written. Huge pages make this worse: one small write can copy 2 MiB.

blocks.question: A machine has 16 GiB of RAM, no swap and `vm.overcommit_memory = 0`. Processes A and B each malloc 12 GiB and each writes only its first 1 GiB. What most likely happens?
options: B's malloc returns NULL because 24 GiB exceeds RAM
Both mallocs succeed and both run normally: only touched pages use RAM
Both succeed, then the OOM killer immediately kills one of them
The kernel zeroes 24 GiB at malloc time and the machine swaps
blocks.explain: The default heuristic only rejects a single request bigger than RAM plus swap; 12 GiB is not, and it does not add up other processes' reservations. Frames are allocated on first touch, so about 2 GiB of RAM is used. Only if A and B actually wrote more than RAM holds would the OOM killer step in.
